children: OTTAWA--A growing number of Canadian exporters are looking to enter new markets even as confidence is growing at home as businesses search for ways to rebalance what has traditionally been a heavy exposure to the U.S., a survey by the country's export credit agency finds.
The poll found that 72% of exporters plan to enter new markets over the next two years, up from 65% five months ago, Export Development Canada said.
The main motivation for broadening outward is to add revenue streams and widen exporters' customer base. Europe and the Asia-Pacific region were identified as the most attractive destinations.

The poll was conducted between June 8 and July 27, after President Trump threatened new tariffs on certain imports from Canada but before the levies were imposed in late August. The survey, done twice a year since 1999, offers a pulse check on levels of confidence and expectations for international trade opportunities over the coming six months.

Export Development Canada said exporters in the country are reporting weakening demand in the U.S., with nearly one-third seeing a decline in orders over the past six months. Looking ahead, 42% of those surveyed anticipate sales will remain at lower levels and 21% expect sales to fall further in the U.S. over the next six months.

Foreign-investment activity also is growing as businesses look for ways to diversify beyond exports, with 34% of exporters surveyed currently investing outside Canada against 25% at the end of 2025. And exporters are responding by increasing sales within Canada, sourcing locally and accepting lower profit margins, the agency said.

The most confident exporters are those chasing a broader trade strategy that combines exports and imports with other forms of trade integration, including domestic sources and investing in capacity both in Canada and abroad, the agency said.
More than half of exporters surveyed expect domestic sales to increase over the next six months, up from 48% at the end of last year.

The U.S. on Aug. 22 imposed new 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods representing about 5% of exports to the U.S. after trade talks between the countries broke down. Prime Minister Mark Carney's government plans to retaliate with a tariff package of its own, with duties ranging from 15% to 50% on an equivalent value of U.S. goods, effective next Tuesday.

The Bank of Canada doesn't expect the new U.S. levies will have a large direct effect on the broader economy, and support programs introduced by Ottawa will likely mitigate some of the damage, though it has warned added uncertainty could lead businesses to delay investment and hiring decisions.

A survey released Thursday by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business found one in five small exporters and 11% of importers affected by the Canada-U.S. trade war expect to stop being financially viable if the conflict lasts three months or more. Just under half of small exporters and a similar number of importers have products directly affected by the latest round of tariffs and counter-tariffs, with manufacturers, wholesalers, retailers and construction businesses among the most affected, accord to the survey.

Data released Thursday by Statistics Canada showed that Canadian exports fell 2.3% between June and July, the first fall in six months after the value of shipments hit a record in June. Exports to the U.S., Canada's largest market by far, were down 6.6% for the month while exports to countries other that the U.S. rose 7.4% to reach the highest on record.
